label: Bonus Class 3
title: Where English Words Come From
bigIdea: English is a Germanic language that borrowed thousands of words from French, Latin, Greek and many others, including Arabic; that is why it often has two words for one idea, an everyday one and a formal one.
bigIdeaAr: الإنجليزية لغة جرمانية استعارت آلاف الكلمات من الفرنسية واللاتينية واليونانية وغيرها، ومنها العربية؛ ولهذا كثيراً ما نجد فيها كلمتين لفكرة واحدة: كلمة يومية وكلمة رسمية.
builtOn: Lesson 9: predictions (succeed, graduate, travel, invent, achieve, discover, cure, technology, solution)
Lesson 10: rules at home (trust, chores, curfew, manners, allowed, independent, privacy, respect, errand)
Lesson 11: the way we talk (clearly, politely, honestly, kindly, tone, body language, eye contact)
Lesson 12: which is better? (option, reasonable, convenient, reliable, affordable, durable, efficient, worth it)
Bonus Classes 1-2: the history of will, must and -ly

objectives.en: I can explain that English is a Germanic language and Arabic is a Semitic language, and name some of their 'relatives'.
objectives.ar: أستطيع أن أشرح أن الإنجليزية لغة جرمانية والعربية لغة سامية، وأن أذكر بعض 'أقاربهما'.

objectives.en: I can describe the main layers of English: Old English, Viking, French, Latin and Greek, and global borrowings.
objectives.ar: أستطيع أن أصف الطبقات الرئيسية للإنجليزية: الإنجليزية القديمة والفايكنج والفرنسية واللاتينية واليونانية والاستعارات العالمية.

objectives.en: I can trace at least six English words that came into English through Arabic and show their route on a map.
objectives.ar: أستطيع أن أتتبع ست كلمات إنجليزية على الأقل دخلت الإنجليزية عن طريق العربية، وأن أبيّن طريقها على الخريطة.

objectives.en: I can choose between an everyday word and a formal word (buy / purchase, ask / inquire) depending on the situation.
objectives.ar: أستطيع أن أختار بين الكلمة اليومية والكلمة الرسمية (buy / purchase, ask / inquire) حسب الموقف.

keyTerms.meaning: The study of where words come from and how their form and meaning changed.
A group of languages that grew from one older 'parent' language.
The branch of languages that includes English, German, Dutch and Swedish.
The branch of languages that includes Arabic, Hebrew, Amharic and Maltese.
A word taken from another language: English 'coffee', Arabic 'كمبيوتر'.
How formal or informal our language is: buy (everyday) vs purchase (formal).
A word whose parts come from different languages: afford (Old English) + -able (French/Latin).

linguisticsCorner.title: Family trees and layers: the life story of English
linguisticsCorner.titleAr: شجرة العائلة والطبقات: قصة حياة الإنجليزية

facts.en: Languages have families. English belongs to the West Germanic branch of the Indo-European family, with German, Dutch and Frisian. Its distant cousins include French, Spanish, Russian, Hindi and even Persian. Arabic belongs to the Semitic branch of the Afro-Asiatic family, with Hebrew, Aramaic, Amharic and Maltese.
facts.ar: للغات عائلات. الإنجليزية تنتمي إلى الفرع الجرماني الغربي من العائلة الهندية الأوروبية، مع الألمانية والهولندية والفريزية. ومن أبناء عمومتها البعيدين: الفرنسية والإسبانية والروسية والهندية بل والفارسية. أما العربية فتنتمي إلى الفرع السامي من العائلة الأفريقية الآسيوية، مع العبرية والآرامية والأمهرية والمالطية.

facts.en: Surprise: Persian is written in Arabic letters and has many Arabic words, but it is related to English, not to Arabic! Compare Persian pedar, mādar, barādar with English father, mother, brother.
facts.ar: مفاجأة: الفارسية تُكتب بالحروف العربية وفيها كلمات عربية كثيرة، لكنها قريبة من الإنجليزية لا من العربية! قارن 'پدر، مادر، برادر' بـ father, mother, brother.

facts.en: English grew in layers. About 1,500 years ago the Angles and Saxons brought Old English (house, water, eat, good). Viking settlers added Old Norse words (sky, egg, knife, they, trust; window = 'wind-eye'). After the Norman Conquest of 1066, French was the language of the rulers for about 300 years, and thousands of French words came in (court, government, manners, curfew). In the Renaissance, scholars added Latin and Greek words (independent, technology).
facts.ar: نمت الإنجليزية على طبقات. قبل نحو 1500 سنة جلب الأنجلز والساكسون الإنجليزية القديمة (house, water, eat, good). ثم أضاف مستوطنو الفايكنج كلمات من النوردية القديمة (sky, egg, knife, they, trust؛ وwindow تعني 'عين الريح'). وبعد الغزو النورماندي سنة 1066 صارت الفرنسية لغة الحكّام نحو 300 سنة، فدخلت آلاف الكلمات الفرنسية (court, government, manners, curfew). وفي عصر النهضة أضاف العلماء كلمات لاتينية ويونانية (independent, technology).

facts.en: Counting dictionary words, only about a quarter of English vocabulary is Germanic; most of the rest is French and Latin. But in real speech the picture flips: almost all of the 100 most frequent English words (the, is, and, have, you, it) are Germanic.
facts.ar: إذا عددنا كلمات القاموس فإن نحو ربع المفردات الإنجليزية فقط جرماني، ومعظم الباقي فرنسي ولاتيني. لكن في الكلام الحقيقي تنقلب الصورة: تقريباً كل الكلمات المئة الأكثر استخداماً (the, is, and, have, you, it) جرمانية.

facts.en: Arabic words reached English mostly in the Middle Ages and later, usually indirectly: through Latin translations of Arabic science (made in places like Toledo in Spain), through Spanish (al-Andalus), through Italian merchants (Venice, Genoa) and through Turkish. Arabic itself had borrowed some of them first (sugar from Persian, which took it from Sanskrit).
facts.ar: وصلت الكلمات العربية إلى الإنجليزية غالباً في العصور الوسطى وما بعدها، وبطريق غير مباشر في الأغلب: عبر الترجمات اللاتينية للعلوم العربية (في مدن مثل طليطلة في إسبانيا)، وعبر الإسبانية (الأندلس)، وعبر التجار الإيطاليين (البندقية وجنوة)، وعبر التركية. وبعض هذه الكلمات استعارته العربية نفسها قبل ذلك (سكر من الفارسية التي أخذتها من السنسكريتية).

arabicBridge.english: Germanic, Indo-European: words grow by adding pieces (kind, kindly, kindness, unkind)
arabicBridge.arabic: سامية، أفريقية آسيوية: الكلمات تُبنى من جذر ووزن (ك ت ب ← كاتب، مكتوب، مكتبة)
arabicBridge.point: The two languages are not related, so similar-looking words are usually borrowings, not 'cousins'. English builds words like LEGO (adding pieces to a stem); Arabic builds them like a mould (root + pattern).
arabicBridge.pointAr: اللغتان ليستا من عائلة واحدة، لذا فالكلمات المتشابهة غالباً مستعارة لا 'قريبة'. الإنجليزية تبني الكلمات مثل الليغو (إضافة قطع إلى أصل)، والعربية تبنيها مثل القالب (جذر + وزن).

arabicBridge.english: sugar, coffee, cotton, algebra, zero, giraffe, sofa, magazine, admiral
arabicBridge.arabic: سكر، قهوة، قطن، الجبر، صفر، زرافة، صُفّة، مخازن، أمير البحر
arabicBridge.point: Arabic gave English hundreds of words, many of them in science, trade and food. Often the Arabic article al- came with them: algebra, alcohol, algorithm, alchemy.
arabicBridge.pointAr: أعطت العربية الإنجليزية مئات الكلمات، كثير منها في العلوم والتجارة والطعام. وغالباً جاءت معها أداة التعريف 'ال': algebra, alcohol, algorithm, alchemy.

arabicBridge.point: Borrowing goes both ways. Arabic took many modern words from English and French, and Arabic academies also create native words for them (حاسوب، هاتف محمول، حافلة).
arabicBridge.pointAr: الاستعارة في الاتجاهين. أخذت العربية كلمات حديثة كثيرة من الإنجليزية والفرنسية، وتصنع المجامع اللغوية العربية أيضاً كلمات أصيلة بديلة (حاسوب، هاتف محمول، حافلة).

arabicBridge.point: Arabic and English share some words because both borrowed them from Greek. Arabic fits borrowed words into its own patterns: تلفن / يتلفن, فبرك.
arabicBridge.pointAr: تشترك العربية والإنجليزية في بعض الكلمات لأن كلتيهما أخذتها من اليونانية. والعربية تُدخل الكلمات المستعارة في أوزانها: تلفن / يتلفن، فبرك.

arabicBridge.english: buy / purchase, help / assist, ask / inquire
arabicBridge.arabic: اشترى / ابتاع، ساعد / عاون، سأل / استفسر
arabicBridge.point: Arabic also has everyday and formal choices, but they mostly come from the same language. In English the formal word is very often French or Latin, and the everyday word Germanic.
arabicBridge.pointAr: في العربية أيضاً اختيار بين كلمة يومية وكلمة رسمية، لكنهما غالباً من اللغة نفسها. أما في الإنجليزية فالكلمة الرسمية كثيراً ما تكون فرنسية أو لاتينية، واليومية جرمانية.

commonErrors.wrong: Arabic and English are sister languages because 'sugar' sounds like 'سكر'.
commonErrors.right: Arabic and English are not related; sugar is a borrowing.
commonErrors.why: Similar words can come from borrowing, not from a shared parent. Real relatives share basic words (mother/Mutter/مادر in Persian), grammar and sound changes.

commonErrors.wrong: I want to purchase a sandwich, bro.
commonErrors.right: I want to buy a sandwich.
commonErrors.why: Mixing registers: purchase is formal (signs, emails, shops' websites). With friends, use the everyday Germanic word.

commonErrors.wrong: Please, I want to inquire you about the homework. (to a friend)
commonErrors.right: Can I ask you about the homework?
commonErrors.why: inquire is formal and takes 'about' (inquire about), not a direct person object. Learners pick the 'bigger' word to sound clever.

commonErrors.wrong: the magazine (meaning a storeroom or a shop)
commonErrors.why: False friend: مخزن and French magasin (shop) are related, but English magazine now means a printed or online publication (and the part of a gun that holds bullets).
The Arabic al- is already inside the English word; do not add another article: not 'the algebra' for the school subject.

commonErrors.wrong: I will commence my homework now. (casual chat)
commonErrors.right: I'm going to start my homework now.
commonErrors.why: commence is very formal (ceremonies, official notices). Everyday speech uses start or begin.

teacher: Language family tree slide (Indo-European and Afro-Asiatic branches, with blank leaves to fill)
Word-origin timeline slide: 450 Old English / 800-1000 Vikings / 1066 Norman French / 1500-1650 Latin and Greek / 1600s-today global words
Route map slide: Baghdad, Cairo, al-Andalus (Toledo, Córdoba), Sicily, Venice, Genoa, Istanbul, Paris, London, Zanzibar, with arrows students can draw with the Teams annotation tool
Word cards for the detective game (sugar, coffee, cotton, algebra, algorithm, zero, giraffe, sofa, magazine, admiral, alcohol, safari)
student: Paper and a pen (or the annotation tool on the shared slide)
A phone or a dictionary app that shows word origins (optional, for the challenge)

stages.name: Warm-up: Hidden Arabic
stages.purpose: Make students notice that English already contains Arabic, and raise the question 'how did it get there?'.
teacherSays: Listen to a short story. Raise your hand every time you hear a word that sounds a bit Arabic to you.

'On Saturday morning, Hamad sat on the sofa with a cup of coffee with lots of sugar. He was reading a magazine about a safari in Kenya, where he saw a giraffe. Then he opened his algebra homework: question one was zero out of ten!'
How many did you find? Write them in the chat. Today we are word detectives: where do English words come from, and how did Arabic words travel to London?
teacherSaysAr: استمعوا للقصة وارفعوا أيديكم كلما سمعتم كلمة تشبه العربية.
اليوم نحن محققو كلمات: من أين جاءت الكلمات الإنجليزية؟ وكيف سافرت الكلمات العربية إلى لندن؟
studentsDo: Listen twice and raise a hand at 'Arabic-sounding' words.
Write the words in the chat (sofa, coffee, sugar, magazine, safari, giraffe, algebra, zero).
Guess the Arabic word behind each one.
tips: Do not confirm all answers yet; keep the suspense for the detective stage.
If students suggest a wrong word (e.g. 'Saturday'), praise the guess and save it: Saturday is from Latin Saturn, a great discussion point later.

stages.name: Linguistics Corner: The Family Tree of Languages
stages.method: Visual discovery (family tree) + evidence from basic words
stages.purpose: Understand language families, place English and Arabic in different families, and learn how linguists prove two languages are related.
teacherSays: Languages have families, like people. How do linguists know two languages are related? They compare basic words, words every family has: mother, father, two, three.
Look: English mother, German Mutter, Dutch moeder. English three, German drei, Dutch drie. They are clearly brothers: the Germanic branch.
Now Arabic: ثلاثة, Hebrew shalosh. أم, Hebrew em. Another family: Semitic.
Here is the big surprise. Persian: pedar, mādar, barādar. Father, mother, brother! Persian is written in Arabic letters, but it is English's distant cousin, not Arabic's.
So English and Arabic are not related. When English and Arabic words look alike, it is usually a borrowing: a word that travelled.
teacherSaysAr: للغات عائلات مثل البشر. يقارن اللغويون الكلمات الأساسية: أم، أب، اثنان، ثلاثة.
مفاجأة: الفارسية تُكتب بحروف عربية لكنها قريبة من الإنجليزية!
الإنجليزية والعربية ليستا من عائلة واحدة؛ الكلمات المتشابهة بينهما غالباً مسافرة (مستعارة).
studentsDo: Compare number and family words across 4 languages on the slide and circle the similar sounds.
Place 10 languages on the family tree (exercise).
Explain in one sentence why Persian is a surprise.

exercise.instructions: Put each language on the right branch of the tree.
exercise.instructionsAr: ضع كل لغة على الفرع الصحيح من الشجرة.

items.answer: Afro-Asiatic - Semitic (grew from Arabic, written in Latin letters)

tips: Maltese and Turkish are the 'trick' items: Maltese looks European but is Semitic; Turkish was once written in Arabic letters but belongs to a different family.
Keep it visual and quick; the goal is the concept of families, not memorizing branches.

stages.name: The Word-Origin Timeline: Layers of English
stages.nameAr: خط زمن أصول الكلمات: طبقات الإنجليزية
stages.purpose: Show that English vocabulary arrived in layers, each with a story, using words from Lessons 9-12.
teacherSays: English is like a cake with layers. Layer 1, around the year 450: the Angles and Saxons. They give us everyday words: house, water, eat, good, kind, worth.
Layer 2, from about 800: the Vikings. Words like sky, egg, knife, they, and trust from Lesson 10! window comes from 'wind-eye': a hole for the wind.

Layer 3, 1066: the Normans from France win the Battle of Hastings. For about 300 years, the rulers speak French. Words like court, government, manners and curfew. Curfew comes from French 'cover fire': at night, people had to cover their fires.
Layer 4, the Renaissance: scholars add Latin and Greek: independent, technology, solution.
Layer 5, today: English borrows from everywhere: emoji and tsunami from Japanese, shampoo from Hindi. And travel? From French travailler, 'to work hard'. Travelling used to be really hard work!
teacherSaysAr: curfew أصلها فرنسي ومعناها 'غطِّ النار': في الليل كان على الناس أن يغطوا نيرانهم.
travel من الفرنسية travailler أي 'يعمل بجهد': كان السفر عملاً شاقاً حقاً!
studentsDo: Follow the timeline and repeat one fun fact per layer.
Drag each word to its layer on the timeline slide.
Tell a partner the story of one word (curfew, window or travel).

exercise.instructions: Put each word on the right layer of the timeline.
exercise.instructionsAr: ضع كل كلمة على الطبقة الصحيحة في خط الزمن.

tips: Dates are approximate; give round numbers and focus on the order of the layers.
Link to Lesson 10 vocabulary: curfew, manners and trust come from three different layers.

stages.name: Arabic Bridge: The Etymology Detective Map
stages.nameAr: جسر العربية: خريطة محقق أصول الكلمات
stages.method: Detective game in teams + map annotation (multimodal)
stages.purpose: Trace English words that came through Arabic, find their Arabic source and draw the route they travelled.
teacherSays: Detectives, here is your case file. Each card has an English word. Find the Arabic word behind it and draw its route on the map.

Example: algebra. Arabic: الجبر, from the title of a 9th-century book by al-Khwarizmi in Baghdad. Route: Baghdad, then Latin translators in Spain, then Europe, then English. Fun fact: in old Spanish, an 'algebrista' was a bone-setter, because الجبر also means setting broken bones!

Careful: many words travelled through other languages first: Italian, Spanish, Turkish, French. And some words were not Arabic at the start: sugar came into Arabic from Persian, and earlier from Sanskrit. So we say 'came into English through Arabic'.
Notice the al-: algebra, algorithm, alcohol. That is the Arabic 'ال' travelling inside the word!
teacherSaysAr: أيها المحققون: لكل بطاقة كلمة إنجليزية، ابحثوا عن الكلمة العربية خلفها وارسموا طريقها على الخريطة.
كثير من الكلمات مرّت بلغات أخرى أولاً: الإيطالية والإسبانية والتركية والفرنسية.
لاحظوا 'ال' التعريف داخل الكلمات: algebra, alcohol!
studentsDo: In two teams, solve 12 word cards: Arabic source + route.
Draw the route arrows on the shared map with the annotation tool.
Score: 1 point for the Arabic word, 1 point for the route; the teacher reveals the answers.
Choose the most surprising word and say why.

exercise.instructions: Find the Arabic word and the route into English.
exercise.instructionsAr: اكتشف الكلمة العربية والطريق الذي سلكته إلى الإنجليزية.

items.answer: سكر - via Medieval Latin and French (Arabic took it from Persian shakar, originally Sanskrit)
قهوة - via Turkish kahve and Italian caffè / Dutch koffie
قطن - via Italian cotone and Old French coton
الجبر - from al-Khwarizmi's book title, via Medieval Latin
the name الخوارزمي (al-Khwarizmi) - via Medieval Latin algorismus
صفر - via Medieval Latin and Italian (cipher also comes from صفر)
صُفّة (a raised bench with cushions) - via Turkish and French
مخازن (storehouses) - via Italian magazzino and French magasin
أمير (as in أمير البحر) - via Medieval Latin and Old French amiral
الكحل (a fine powder for the eyes) - via Medieval Latin; the meaning changed completely

tips: Give weaker teams the Arabic words in a jumbled list to match instead of finding them.
Be honest about uncertainty: etymologists sometimes disagree about exact routes; say 'probably via...' when needed.
Extra words for fast teams: lemon (ليمون, from Persian), candy (قند, ultimately Persian/Sanskrit), syrup (شراب), arsenal (دار الصناعة).

stages.name: Two Words for One Idea: Everyday vs Formal
stages.method: Guided discovery of synonym layers + register rewriting
stages.purpose: Understand why English has Germanic everyday words and French/Latin formal words, and choose the right one for the situation.
teacherSays: After 1066, the farmers spoke English and the rulers spoke French. A famous story: the animal in the field kept its English name, but the meat on the rich man's table got a French name. cow - beef, sheep - mutton, calf - veal, deer - venison.

The real history is a bit more complicated, but the pattern is real: English often has an everyday Germanic word and a formal French or Latin word. buy - purchase, help - assist, ask - inquire, start - commence, need - require.
Sometimes there are three! kingly (Germanic), royal (French), regal (Latin). ask, question, interrogate.
Which one do we use? With friends: the short Germanic word. In signs, emails and official texts: the longer French or Latin word.
teacherSaysAr: بعد 1066 تكلم الفلاحون الإنجليزية والحكّام الفرنسية: الحيوان في الحقل اسمه إنجليزي، واللحم على مائدة الغني اسمه فرنسي.
مع الأصدقاء: الكلمة الجرمانية القصيرة. في اللافتات والرسائل الرسمية: الكلمة الفرنسية أو اللاتينية الأطول.
studentsDo: Match everyday words with their formal partners.
Rewrite a formal mall notice in everyday English for a friend, then a friend's message in formal English for an email.
Discuss: which word sounds friendlier? which sounds more serious?

exercise.instructions: Give the everyday word for the formal one, or the formal word for the everyday one.
exercise.instructionsAr: اكتب الكلمة اليومية مقابل الرسمية، أو الرسمية مقابل اليومية.

items.prompt: Formal notice: 'Customers who wish to purchase tickets should inquire at the desk.' -> everyday
items.answer: If you want to buy tickets, ask at the desk.

items.prompt: Everyday: 'Can you help me? I need more time.' -> formal email
items.answer: Could you assist me? I require more time.

tips: Formal is not 'better': using purchase with friends sounds strange or funny. Good English means choosing the right register.
Connect to Arabic: فصحى vs عامية is a similar choice, but English mixes the two layers inside one language every day.

stages.name: Word Biographies and Hybrid Hunters
stages.purpose: Use the new knowledge to tell the life story of one word and find words built from parts of different languages.
teacherSays: Some words are hybrids: their parts come from different languages. affordable = afford (Old English) + -able (French and Latin). useful = use (French) + -ful (Old English). body language = body (Old English) + language (French, from Latin lingua, 'tongue').
Now choose one word from today or from Lessons 9-12 and write its 'passport': Born in... / Arrived in English... / Route... / Old meaning... / Today's meaning...
You have 3 minutes to prepare and 30 seconds to present. Speak clearly and confidently, like a museum guide!
teacherSaysAr: بعض الكلمات هجينة: أجزاؤها من لغات مختلفة.
اختر كلمة واكتب 'جواز سفرها': مكان الولادة، وقت الوصول، الطريق، المعنى القديم، المعنى اليوم.
قدّمها خلال 30 ثانية بوضوح وثقة كمرشد في متحف!
studentsDo: Split 6 words into parts and name the origin of each part.
Write a word passport (5 lines).
Present it in 30 seconds; peers give one 'star' (something good) and one 'wish' (something to improve).

exercise.instructions: Split the word into parts and give the origin of each part.
exercise.instructionsAr: قسّم الكلمة إلى أجزاء واذكر أصل كل جزء.

items.answer: body (Old English) + language (French, from Latin lingua)

tips: Suggested passport words: curfew, travel, window, manners, technology, coffee, algebra, sofa.
Use a simple peer rubric: clear voice, one fact, one route, eye contact.

stages.name: Exit Ticket, Did You Know? and Goodbye
stages.purpose: Check the key ideas (families, layers, Arabic loanwords, register) and send students home with a fact to share.
teacherSays: Exit ticket: five quick questions. Three minutes.

Did you know? The word 'check' in chess comes from Persian shāh, 'king', and 'checkmate' from shāh māt, which reached Europe through Arabic. When you say 'checkmate', you are speaking Persian through Arabic!
Your mission: find three English words in a shop, a menu or an app that came into English through Arabic. Bring them to the next class.
teacherSaysAr: هل تعلم؟ كلمة check في الشطرنج من الفارسية 'شاه' أي الملك، وcheckmate من 'شاه مات' التي وصلت أوروبا عبر العربية!
مهمتك: ابحث عن ثلاث كلمات إنجليزية في متجر أو قائمة طعام أو تطبيق دخلت الإنجليزية عن طريق العربية.
studentsDo: Complete the 5 exit-ticket items.
Say one word and its origin as their goodbye ('Goodbye from algebra, born in Baghdad!').
tips: This class adds no topic vocabulary to test; assess the understanding of families, layers and register.
Collect the mission words for a 'Lumio Word Museum' slide in Bonus Class 4 or Lesson 17.

items.prompt: Is English a Germanic or a Semitic language?
Which event in 1066 brought thousands of French words into English?
True or false: Persian and English are in the same language family.

homework.en: Word Museum: make a mini-museum of 5 English words that came into English through Arabic (or other languages). For each word, write its 'passport' (origin, route, old and new meaning) and draw its route on a small map.
homework.ar: متحف الكلمات: اصنع متحفاً صغيراً لخمس كلمات إنجليزية دخلت الإنجليزية عن طريق العربية (أو لغات أخرى). اكتب لكل كلمة 'جواز سفرها' (الأصل، الطريق، المعنى القديم والجديد) وارسم طريقها على خريطة صغيرة.
tasks: Write 5 word passports and draw one route map.
Find 3 pairs of everyday/formal words in a real sign, email or website (buy/purchase type).
Ask a family member which English words they use in Arabic every day (موبايل، باص...) and list 5.

support: Give the Arabic words for the detective game as a matching list.
Use only three timeline layers: Old English, French (1066), Latin/Greek.
Provide the word passport as a fill-in template with sentence starters.
challenge: Use an online etymology dictionary to trace two Lesson 9-12 words (e.g. efficient, achieve) and present their old meanings.
Find a triplet like kingly / royal / regal (Germanic / French / Latin): e.g. rise / mount / ascend.
Explain why a word's route matters: why does 'coffee' have a different vowel from قهوة? (It changed in Turkish and Italian.)

successCriteria: Places at least 8 of 10 languages on the correct branch of the family tree.
Explains the Norman Conquest layer and gives at least two French-origin words.
Finds the Arabic source of at least 8 of 12 detective words and describes at least three routes.
Switches correctly between everyday and formal words in at least 7 of 9 items.
watchFor: Thinking English and Arabic are related because of loanwords
Using formal words (purchase, commence, inquire) in casual speech
Saying every Arabic-looking word came directly from Arabic (many came via Persian, Turkish, Italian or Spanish)

teacherNotes: Etymologies in this class follow standard dictionaries (Oxford, Merriam-Webster, Etymonline). Where routes are debated, say 'probably'.
The cow/beef story was made famous by the novelist Walter Scott (Ivanhoe); historians say the reality was more mixed, but the Germanic-everyday / French-formal pattern is well established.
The percentages (about a quarter Germanic in the dictionary; almost all of the 100 most common words Germanic) are approximate and depend on the word list used.
Avoid religion or national comparisons ('Arabic is better/older'); the message is that languages share and borrow, and Arabic science shaped European vocabulary.
Bonus Class 4 (The Art of Persuasion) will reuse the formal/everyday choice in speeches and the Greek origin of rhetoric (ethos, pathos, logos).
